brief.head: The Nordic exception
brief.text: Scandinavia’s wel­fare states[[x4]] do not re­fute free mar­kets, Amit Varma said. Those coun­tries grew rich as free mar­kets first, and could af­ford wel­fare statism only af­ter­wards. {010-C16}

brief.head: Nobody designed it
brief.text: Languages, economies and nat­u­ral se­lec­tion[[x6]] need no cen­tral plan­ner, Amit Varma said. They are, in Adam Ferguson’s words, “the prod­ucts of human ac­tion and not human de­sign”[[x5]]. {010-J15}

brief.head: Discovery, not design
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s phrase is “dis­cov­ery, not de­sign”[[x7]]. Poverty has never been ended by cen­tral plan­ners, only by searchers who learn by trial and error, Amit Varma read from William Easterly. {010-C04}

brief.head: Two speeches a week
brief.text: At the fi­nance min­istry, Ajay Shah re­called, every joint sec­re­tary gave two con­fer­ence speeches a week, to show busi­ness a ca­pa­ble crew[[x8]] with a vi­sion and a strat­egy. {010-S10}

brief.head: Not about skin colour
brief.text: Indians once be­lieved “be­cause our skins are brown we’ll never be able to ex­port”, Ajay Shah said. Manmohan Singh’s PhD the­sis[[x9]] ar­gued it was about in­cen­tives, prices and ex­change rates. {010-C10}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why freedom matters
lead.head: Midnight’s unfree children

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 10

body: Amit Varma began by ac­count­ing for the cat. A young cat was mew­ing in the back­ground, he ex­plained, and it sounded “like the wail­ing of all the dis­pos­sessed and the hun­gry and the starv­ing through these many, many years of India’s tor­mented jour­ney”. {010-J01}
India ejected colo­nial rule in 1947, Ajay Shah said, but in many ways free­dom did not then come to the peo­ple. “We ended up with less free­dom in many re­spects.”
Varma agreed. He has long called the un­fin­ished work India’s sec­ond free­dom strug­gle.
## Consent and its fruits

Varma’s case rests on con­sent. “How should I live in this world?” and “how should the state re­late to so­ci­ety?” look like sep­a­rate ques­tions, he said, but they share an an­swer: “con­sent is ev­ery­thing and co­er­cion is the ul­ti­mate evil.” {010-C01}

Freedom, he ar­gued, is also the road to pros­per­ity. Every vol­un­tary ex­change leaves both sides bet­ter off, so the world is not zero-sum. Citing their friend Nitin Pai[[x1]], he said that after 1991 each per­cent­age point of GDP growth lifted three mil­lion Indians out of poverty.

Shah added that peo­ple can sur­vive un­free­dom, even in a con­cen­tra­tion camp, but a so­ci­ety with­out agency stops cre­at­ing. A poor coun­try, he said, needs “an ef­fer­ves­cence of op­ti­mism, of cre­ativ­ity, of in­ven­tion”.
## Booms, busts and a near miss
Shah then walked through India’s his­tory. Its share of pre-industrial world GDP, he said, re­flected good weather and many peo­ple, not riches: “It was not a golden age.”

Modern India, in his telling, began around 1869, when the Suez Canal, the tele­graph, the rail­way and British com­pany law ar­rived al­most at once. Wars, the Depression and Partition dark­ened the years from 1913 to 1947.
After Independence the num­bers looked de­cent, but pol­icy got steadily worse. Controls crept in, and each fail­ure was met with more of them.
Shah re­called the au­dac­ity of 1947: uni­ver­sal suf­frage in a coun­try where women’s lit­er­acy was six per cent. {010-S05}

Between 1962 and 1977 the ex­per­i­ment nearly failed. Three wars, Nehru’s death, droughts, bank na­tion­al­i­sa­tion, dou­ble-digit in­fla­tion and the Emergency left many fear­ing India would be­come “an­other dis­gust­ing au­thor­i­tar­ian third world coun­try”.
Varma, read­ing from Shruti Rajagopalan’s essay on those years, cited a top in­come-tax rate of 97.75 per cent. He thinks the eco­nomic con­trols did more harm than the Emergency.

Recovery began in 1977 under the Janata gov­ern­ment, and Shah said care­ful econo­met­rics dates the ac­cel­er­a­tion of growth to 1979. Varma noted that the re­form­ers of 1991 had been pre­par­ing for a decade and a half.
## The frag­ile years
By 2011 the mo­men­tum had gone. Shah’s sum­mary statis­tic: there was less free­dom in 2010 than in 2000, and less in 2020 than in 2010.

Varma traced the slide to a chain of ac­ci­dents after the Mumbai at­tacks of 2008. Shah found bad luck “a deeply dis­sat­is­fy­ing so­lu­tion”. The re­form­ers, he said, had op­er­ated the old ma­chin­ery of gov­ern­ment more sen­si­bly but never re­built it.
“What was keep­ing the ship aloft were cer­tain in­di­vid­u­als,” he said, “which to me is an un­ac­cept­able and frag­ile way of build­ing a coun­try.” {010-C13}

Varma con­fessed to grow­ing de­spon­dent. Shah urged cau­tion, not de­spair. Bright dawns in China, Russia and Weimar Germany turned ugly, he said, but post-war Germany and Japan be­came “beau­ti­ful coun­tries”.
“The world is a rich and won­der­ful place,” he said, “and progress can al­ways hap­pen.” {010-C15}

second.label: The world before 1914
second.head: No papers, no problem
second.deck: Ajay Shah on freedoms lost to war, and never given back

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the world before passports

body: Before 1914, Ajay Shah said, no­body any­where in the world needed a pass­port[[x2]]. Royals wrote to each other ask­ing favours for their friends, but or­di­nary peo­ple sim­ply trav­elled and mi­grated. {010-S04}

Capital con­trols did not exist until Adolf Hitler[[x3]] in­tro­duced them in Germany. In India, curbs on trade and cap­i­tal flows began as a British wartime mea­sure in 1939. “The loss of free­dom began as wartime mea­sures,” Shah said, and has since been nor­malised.

The Treaty of Versailles had a clause restor­ing pass­port-free travel, and con­fer­ences pur­sued it into the 1960s. Soviet Russia blocked every at­tempt, be­cause it never wanted its peo­ple to leave. Only the European Union has partly re­stored the old free­dom. {010-J04}

quote.text: Did you know that be­fore 1914 there were no pass­ports any­where in the world?

third.head: Malaria’s cold comfort

pic.caption: Amit Varma on gin, tonic and American ice

body: Malaria was a huge prob­lem in India, Amit Varma said, and the de­fence against it was qui­nine. {#malaria}
Quinine could not be had on its own: it was bit­ter and ugly. So it was put into tonic water, and gin and tonic be­came a pop­u­lar cock­tail in India. A gin and tonic needs ice.
This was the 19th cen­tury. “No fridges,” Varma said. “Where will the ice come from? America will make the ice.” And so a bunch of ice fac­to­ries were set up in the American Midwest. {010-S02}

He of­fered it as a com­pan­ion to Ajay Shah’s story of the American Civil War, which cut off cot­ton to Britain and cre­ated a new trade through Bombay. A dis­ease in India built an in­dus­try across the world. “So the won­ders of global cap­i­tal­ism,” Varma said.

box.title: The unwritten book
box.text: Around 2008 Amit Varma pitched *Freedom After Midnight* to the New India Foundation, ar­gu­ing that 1947 brought only po­lit­i­cal free­dom, not per­sonal, so­cial or eco­nomic free­dom. He never wrote it “be­cause I’m a lazy bum”[[x10]], and the pro­posal was re­jected any­way. {010-J02}

sections.label: The first principle
sections.head: Consent is everything
sections.caption: freedom as consent
body: Freedom is such a mis­used word that Amit Varma prefers to think in terms of con­sent. How should I live, and how should the state re­late to so­ci­ety? One ques­tion seems to be­long to ethics and the other to po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy, he said, but both have the same an­swer. {010-C01}

You can reach it from first prin­ci­ples, through in­di­vid­ual au­ton­omy and John Locke’s right to self-ownership, or from con­se­quences, be­cause free­dom gives the best out­comes. Varma also flagged what he calls the grand lib­eral para­dox[[x12]]: to enjoy our rights we need a state, and the state takes some of them away.
## Not a fixed pie

Our brains, he sug­gested, evolved in small tribes in times of scarcity, so we think in zero-sum terms[[x11]]. Angus Maddison’s chart of world GDP tells an­other story: it shoots up around 1800. The rea­son, Varma said, is that every vol­un­tary trans­ac­tion leaves both peo­ple bet­ter off, so the more of them there are, the richer the world be­comes. {010-C02}

That makes free­dom a hu­man­i­tar­ian cause: he cred­ited the 1991 re­forms with bring­ing 300 to 400 mil­lion peo­ple out of poverty. Yet about 70 per cent of India was born after the Berlin Wall fell, and the young have for­got­ten the hor­rors of so­cial­ism. {#berlin}
~ Ajay Shah added what un­free­dom costs. People sur­vive it, even in a con­cen­tra­tion camp, but once agency is taken away, the arts, sci­ence and busi­ness sink into “a dull de­spon­dence”.

quote.text: The an­swer is con­sent. That con­sent is ev­ery­thing and co­er­cion is the ul­ti­mate evil.

sections.label: Before 1947
sections.head: A golden age that wasn’t
sections.caption: India before Independence
body: India’s large share of world GDP be­fore in­dus­tri­al­i­sa­tion is no cause for nos­tal­gia, Ajay Shah said. It re­flected good weather and a big pop­u­la­tion, and out­put per per­son was abysmal ev­ery­where. Old India had “very lit­tle po­lit­i­cal de­vel­op­ment” and “no rule of law”. {010-C06}

Modernity came, in his ac­count, in the 1860s and 1870s, and it lasted until 1913. Then came a long dark pe­riod: two world wars, the Great Depression, the un­rest of the free­dom move­ment and the hor­rors of Partition, with British poli­cies often hos­tile to the Indian econ­omy.
## A re­turn, not a rup­ture

Amit Varma read from the his­to­rian Tirthankar Roy’s essay: the em­pire cre­ated an econ­omy open to trade, cap­i­tal flows and set­tle­ment, and eco­nomic na­tion­al­ists mis­read pay­ments to Britain as a “drain”[[x13]] when they were the price of tap­ping a mo­bile mar­ket for skills and cap­i­tal.

Varma also re­layed an ar­gu­ment from Vinay Sitapati: 1991 should be seen as a re-liberalisation, be­cause it was Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism and cen­tral plan­ning that broke with the past. {010-C07}
~ Sitapati draws too on Richard Eaton’s *India in the Persianate Age*, which sug­gests that global trade moved power to the port cities and weak­ened the cen­tralised em­pire. {010-R07}

quote.text: We should think of the lib­er­al­i­sa­tion of ninety one as a re-liberalisation of ninety one.

sections.label: 1947 to 1962
sections.head: An empty seat for Laski
sections.caption: the planners of 1947
body: India in 1947 was freer than its later his­tory sug­gests, Ajay Shah said. State in­ter­ven­tion was mod­est, the level of free­dom was rel­a­tively high, and “we’ve never had a bet­ter civil ser­vice in India than was present in 1947”. {010-S03}
Then, day after day, re­stric­tions crept in. Amit Varma traced the mind­set be­hind them. Nehru told J.R.D. Tata: “Do not speak to me of profit[[x14]], it is a dirty word.” {010-J09}

A 1951 *Time* mag­a­zine piece called Beatrice and Sidney Webb, the god­par­ents of Fabian so­cial­ism[[x15]], “in a truer sense his cre­ators than Vishnu and Shiva”. A wit quoted by Ramachandra Guha said that at every cab­i­net meet­ing “there was an empty seat and Harold Laski sat on it”. {010-J11}
## Wrong, and stay­ing wrong

Varma saw three cen­tral­is­ing im­pulses in 1947: po­lit­i­cal, as the coun­try seemed to fall apart; so­cial, as Ambedkar saw vil­lages as dens of lo­cal­ism; and eco­nomic, in Nehru’s dis­trust of profit. The mis­take, he said, was be­liev­ing a lib­eral so­ci­ety could be im­posed from the top down. {010-C08}

~ Shah’s com­plaint was not that the plan­ners were wrong but that they would not change course. Some of the smartest peo­ple avail­able an­swered every fail­ure with more con­trols, in­sist­ing that “the flog­gings will con­tinue until the morale im­proves”.

quote.text: It is okay to be wrong. It is not okay to be im­per­vi­ous to the ev­i­dence.

sections.label: 1962 to 1977
sections.head: Fifteen years on the brink
sections.caption: the terrifying years
body: India in 1947 was “a pre­co­cious po­lit­i­cal project”, Ajay Shah said: uni­ver­sal suf­frage in a coun­try where women’s lit­er­acy was six per cent. {010-S05}

Then came the China war of 1962, Nehru’s death in 1964, war with Pakistan in 1965, two droughts in a row, famine, and beg­ging the United States for PL 480 food aid. The banks were na­tion­alised in 1969. The 1971 war was “a na­tion­al­ist wet dream”, he said, but an enor­mous eco­nomic bur­den.

The eu­pho­ria of the Bangladesh war and Indira Gandhi’s big elec­tion win gave way to dou­ble-digit in­fla­tion, the JP ag­i­ta­tion and the Emergency[[x16]]. She was, Shah noted, the first Indian prime min­is­ter whom po­lit­i­cal sci­en­tists clas­sify as a pop­ulist.
## Worse than the Emergency
Amit Varma, quot­ing Shruti Rajagopalan, listed tar­iffs above 350 per cent on some goods and the na­tion­al­i­sa­tion of the 14 largest banks. The top in­come-tax rate was 97.75 per cent. {#tax}
Indira did not even be­lieve in this so­cial­ism, Varma ar­gued; she used it to tilt left against the syn­di­cate. Her eco­nomic reg­u­la­tions, he said, were far worse than the Emergency. {#worse}

~ Democracy sur­vived partly through em­bar­rass­ment. Leaked diplo­matic ma­te­rial, Shah said, shows Indira was em­bar­rassed about the Emergency, and the 1977 elec­tions were truly free and fair. {010-S07}

quote.text: It was only Sanjay Gandhi’s mother who could have de­clared the emer­gency, and it was only Jawaharlal Nehru’s daugh­ter who could have de­clared elec­tions.

sections.label: 1977 onwards
sections.head: Three Gujaratis turn the ship
sections.caption: the long road to 1991
body: In 1977 the Janata Party put three Gujaratis in charge: Morarji Desai as prime min­is­ter, H.M. Patel as fi­nance min­is­ter and D.T. Lakdawala as deputy chair­man of the Planning Commission. They were not rad­i­cal re­form­ers, Ajay Shah said, but they had an in­stinct for mar­kets.

Lakdawala had al­ways been at Bombay University, far from Delhi’s left­ist eco­nom­ics es­tab­lish­ment, and Patel had grown up near Amul and the co­op­er­a­tive move­ment. Small mea­sures and key staffing choices began “a gen­tle process of turn­ing the ship”.

Growth, Shah ar­gued, comes only from the pri­vate sec­tor[[x17]] com­mit­ting its hours, its chil­dren and its money to build­ing firms, and it does so when it feels safe about where India is head­ing. {010-C11}
The mood turned quickly: care­ful econo­met­rics dates India’s growth ac­cel­er­a­tion to 1979. {#growth1979}
## Bug re­ports and land­mines

From 1991 to 2011, Shah said, the state was full of land­mines, but busi­nesses that hit one could “file a bug re­port” and often get it fixed. That com­pact among India’s four elites broke down as the state’s deeds fell short of its words. {010-C12}

~ The re­form­ers, he said, had run an old, re­pres­sive ap­pa­ra­tus with­out re­build­ing it. His coun­terex­am­ple was the United States under Donald Trump, where much of gov­ern­ment worked as usual: “That is in­sti­tu­tional qual­ity.”

quote.text: Always and al­ways and al­ways there is only one source of eco­nomic growth and that is the pri­vate sec­tor.
People should not ask for fate to step out of the page of his­tory and shake your hand. People should just be quiet and dig in and work hard and you have no right to ask for any re­ward.

p3.title: Stories from the road
p3.deck: Canals, scooters, homecomings and a reshuffle: the tales behind India’s history

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the decade that wired India to the world
stories.head: The short cut to modernity
body: Modern India did not begin in 1947, or in 1991, in Ajay Shah’s telling. It began in the 1860s and 1870s, and above all in 1869.

That year the Suez Canal started work­ing[[x18]], and the dis­tance be­tween London and Bombay came down dra­mat­i­cally. {#suez} Before it, a ship from London went around the Cape of Good Hope, and hav­ing come that far might as well carry on to Calcutta. After it, the route ran through the Straits of Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, “and boom, you are at Bombay”.

The tele­graph ar­rived too. When the first con­nec­tions reached Bombay in the 1860s, a mes­sage took about four hours be­tween the two cities, so that cot­ton spec­u­la­tors could talk to each other. {#telegraph}

So did the rail­road, and so did the legal plumb­ing of a mar­ket econ­omy. The Companies Act, the Contract Act and the Evidence Act all came to India; the Companies Act reached Bombay within a cou­ple of years of pass­ing in London. In 1874 came the Bombay Stock Exchange. {#bse}
Then the American Civil War cut off cot­ton sup­plies from America to Britain. A whole cot­ton trade was in­vented in India: grown in Gujarat and Maharashtra, shipped through Bombay to London.
“It’s like the en­tire in­sti­tu­tional pack­age and the tech­no­log­i­cal ca­pa­bil­ity of the Industrial Revolution was seeded into India all at once,” Shah said. {010-S01}

~ This first mod­erni­sa­tion, which co­in­cides with what is called the first glob­al­i­sa­tion, ran roughly from 1869 to 1913. Shah thinks it goes un­recog­nised in India, not least be­cause the na­tion­al­ists over­sold their case.
stories.why: Modern India is older than its usual birth­days. Connectivity, tech­nol­ogy and the in­sti­tu­tions of a mar­ket econ­omy ar­rived to­gether in a sin­gle burst, and the Indian econ­omy had an ex­plo­sive mo­ment, until wars and the Depression closed the world again.
stories.postscript: He does not pine for colo­nial rule, Shah said. But his­tory should be read “cold and clear”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the year India was wired in

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the economics of the Indira years
stories.head: The bride wore a waiting list
body: By the time Indira Gandhi took of­fice, Amit Varma read from Shruti Rajagopalan’s essay, the of­fi­cial goal was to na­tion­alise all means of pro­duc­tion. Her gov­ern­ment na­tion­alised the 14 largest banks overnight by or­di­nance, along with coal and cop­per mines and gen­eral in­sur­ance.[[x20]]

Some goods faced im­port tar­iffs above 350 per cent. The top in­come-tax rate was 97.75 per cent. {#tax} By the late 1970s it was al­most im­pos­si­ble to start a busi­ness, or to exit a fail­ing one.
Scarcity bred jokes. Parents of a girl were told to book a scooter early[[x19]], so that it would be de­liv­ered by the time of her wed­ding. {010-S06}

~ Varma thinks Indira did not even be­lieve in this so­cial­ism, and that her eco­nomic reg­u­la­tions kept mil­lions in poverty for decades longer than nec­es­sary, stop­ping a labour-intensive man­u­fac­tur­ing boom that could have come be­fore China’s.

quote.text: India was the one coun­try in the world where a sec­ond­hand car cost more than a new car.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on booking a scooter for a wedding

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the reformers who dug in
stories.head: Sharpening axes in the dark
body: Ajay Shah sees two dark stretches in mod­ern Indian his­tory. From 1927 to 1947 the British Empire looked in­fin­itely pow­er­ful, yet the best Indians dug in, wrote long­hand let­ters and ar­gued about what India should be.
From 1962 to 1977 the same story played out. Shah was born in 1966 and has heard about those years from his el­ders. {#born1966} Many peo­ple gave up and left the coun­try.

Manmohan Singh came home after his PhD with no prom­ise that he would be fi­nance min­is­ter or prime min­is­ter. “Nobody would have bet on a mil­lion to one odds that this was going to hap­pen,” Shah said. {010-S09}

~ Montek Singh Ahluwalia, Amit Varma added, left the World Bank[[x21]] when Singh asked him to come back. Vijay Kelkar, Shah said[[x22]], “just felt obliged to say, Yes, sir, I will,” and packed his bags.
stories.why: Big re­forms rest on years of un­re­warded prepa­ra­tion by peo­ple who chose to stay. Varma reached for Abraham Lincoln’s line: with six hours to cut a tree, spend the first five sharp­en­ing the axe. {010-J14}
stories.postscript: Just as we re­mem­ber those who fought, Varma said, we should re­mem­ber those who did not. Most peo­ple, Shah replied, were sim­ply ap­peasers.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the reformers who came home

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how a terror attack derailed the economy
stories.head: Home calls, Finance empties
body: In 2008-09, Amit Varma said, ev­ery­thing was going well. Manmohan Singh was prime min­is­ter, P. Chidambaram was fi­nance min­is­ter, and India was han­dling the global fi­nan­cial cri­sis ca­pa­bly. Then came the ter­ror­ist at­tacks on Mumbai.

The home min­is­ter, Shivraj Patil, was un­able to han­dle it. “Manmohan Singh wanted his best man on the job, that was Chidambaram,” Varma said. “That meant the fi­nance min­istry was now empty.” {010-S11}

Singh would have taken Finance him­self, but he had to have an op­er­a­tion that January. Sonia Gandhi put Pranab Mukherjee in the post, a so­cial­ist thinker, Varma said, from the Indira 70s. Retrospective tax­a­tion fol­lowed[[x23]], and around 2013 Mukherjee was kicked up­stairs to the pres­i­dency.
~ Chidambaram re­turned. After 2014 the Jaitley min­istry showed con­ti­nu­ity for a while, then pol­i­tics took over: from 2015, Varma said, “ev­ery­thing goes to hell”.
stories.why: Ajay Shah re­jected the bad-luck story. A chain of ac­ci­dents can de­rail an econ­omy only if ev­ery­thing de­pends on who sits in which chair, he ar­gued; the an­swer is to write free­dom into laws and or­gan­i­sa­tion de­sign. {010-C13}

quiz.q: Which waterway, opened in 1869, cut the sea route from London to Bombay?
quiz.a: The Suez Canal, send­ing ships via Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

quiz.q: Why, by Amit Varma’s account, did ice factories spring up in the American Midwest?
quiz.a: Malaria in India meant qui­nine, tonic water, gin and tonic, and so ice.

quiz.q: Who, according to Ajay Shah, introduced the world’s first capital controls?
quiz.a: Adolf Hitler, in Germany; be­fore 1914 no­body needed pass­ports ei­ther.

quiz.q: What did Nehru tell J.R.D. Tata about profit, as Varma quoted it?
quiz.a: “Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.”

quiz.q: Which three Gujaratis became India’s most powerful people in 1977?
quiz.a: Morarji Desai, H.M. Patel and D.T. Lakdawala, under the Janata gov­ern­ment.

quiz.q: Why did the finance ministry fall empty after the 2008 Mumbai attacks?
quiz.a: Manmohan Singh moved P. Chidambaram to Home to re­place Shivraj Patil.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 10. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Indira Gandhi (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India); Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); John Locke (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); Harold Laski (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Morarji Desai (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); William Easterly (Jerry Bauer, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Sixteen Stormy Days
shelf.creator: Tripurdaman Singh
shelf.why: The de­fin­i­tive ac­count of India’s First Amendment, which, un­like America’s, was a blow against free speech: the Lok Sabha de­bates show Nehru tak­ing il­lib­eral po­si­tions to si­lence his ri­vals, a great states­man un­done by hubris.

shelf.title: Nehru: The Debates that Defined India
shelf.creator: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
shelf.why: Nehru’s de­bates with Jinnah, Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Patel show fine minds dis­agree­ing in good faith over power and rights, a spirit of ‘as­sume goodwill’, lost in today’s dis­course, that Amit finds deeply in­spir­ing.

shelf.title: The quest for economic freedom in India
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: He calls it ‘ab­so­lutely magisterial’.

shelf.title: The 1991 Project
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan / Mercatus Center
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan’s trea­sure trove of chron­i­cles and oral his­to­ries of the 1991 re­forms, in­clud­ing the leg­endary ‘M document’.

shelf.title: The Economic Legacies of Colonial Rule in India
shelf.creator: Tirthankar Roy
shelf.why: A ‘fab­u­lous essay’ ar­gu­ing the colo­nial econ­omy was open to trade, cap­i­tal and mi­gra­tion.

shelf.title: Planners vs. Searchers in Foreign Aid
shelf.creator: William Easterly
shelf.why: It frames the key con­trast: plan­ners im­pose top-down an­swers, while searchers find so­lu­tions by trial, error and feed­back.

shelf.title: India in the Persianate Age
shelf.creator: Richard Eaton
shelf.why: A ‘mag­nif­i­cent book’ adored by the Mughal his­to­ri­ans on Amit’s show.

shelf.title: Half-Lion: How PV Narasimha Rao Transformed India
shelf.creator: Vinay Sitapati
shelf.why: Sitapati’s bi­og­ra­phy of Narasimha Rao, which shows him as a great man of learn­ing and con­stant rein­ven­tion who staked his po­lit­i­cal cap­i­tal on the 1991 re­forms, not just a politi­cian who hap­pened to be there.

shelf.title: Jugalbandi: The BJP Before Modi
shelf.creator: Vinay Sitapati
shelf.why: Same en­thu­si­asm for Sitapati’s work as an in­ter­preter of post-Independence po­lit­i­cal his­tory.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Manmohan Singh’s PhD thesis
shelf.creator: Manmohan Singh
shelf.why: One of the first works to chal­lenge India’s ‘ex­port pessimism’.

shelf.title: Arun Shourie’s books
shelf.creator: Arun Shourie
shelf.why: Ajay says Shourie ‘does not get enough recognition’.

shelf.title: Angus Maddison’s world GDP charts
shelf.creator: Angus Maddison
shelf.why: They show world GDP shoot­ing up around 1800 and eco­nomic free­dom track­ing pros­per­ity coun­try by coun­try, in­clud­ing India after 1991 and China after Deng.

shelf.title: The Double ‘Thank You’ Moment
shelf.creator: John Stossel
shelf.why: Stossel’s sim­plest pic­ture of pos­i­tive-sum ex­change: when you buy a cof­fee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, be­cause both are bet­ter off.

shelf.title: The End of History?
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: Fukuyama’s essay cap­tures the post-1989 be­lief that lib­eral democ­racy had won the ar­gu­ment for good.

shelf.title: How Laissez-Faire Made Sweden Rich
shelf.creator: Johan Norberg
shelf.why: Norberg shows in de­tail that the Nordic coun­tries got rich as free-market economies first and built their wel­fare states af­ter­wards: Amit’s an­swer to peo­ple who cite Scandinavia against the case for free­dom.

shelf.title: Passports Were a ‘Temporary’ War Measure
shelf.creator: Speranta Dumitru
shelf.why: Covers the his­tory be­hind his point that pass­ports and con­trols on move­ment began as wartime mea­sures and were never rolled back.

shelf.title: Pandit’s Mind (1951 Time magazine cover story on Nehru)
shelf.creator: Time magazine
shelf.why: A vivid por­trait of how Fabian so­cial­ism and Brahminical con­tempt for the ‘Banya’ shaped Nehru’s dis­trust of cap­i­tal­ism.

shelf.title: India’s Founding Moment
shelf.creator: Madhav Khosla
shelf.why: Helps ex­plain the elite, top-down mind­set of the founders, who felt they had to teach the na­tion how to think.

shelf.title: The Lost Decade
shelf.creator: Puja Mehra
shelf.why: Puja Mehra’s ac­count of how India’s growth stalled after 2008, through de­ci­sions like ret­ro­spec­tive tax­a­tion and the reshuf­fle that made Pranab Mukherjee fi­nance min­is­ter.

shelf.title: The Clash of Economic Ideas
shelf.creator: Lawrence H White
shelf.why: Lawrence White’s his­tory of the big eco­nomic de­bates of the last cen­tury, from Keynes and Friedman to Fabian so­cial­ism and cen­tral plan­ning, show­ing that each school was right in some ways and wrong in oth­ers.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: India’s Greatest Civil Servant (Episode 167, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Narayani Basu
shelf.why: Narayani Basu on V.P.

shelf.title: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (Episode 283, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
shelf.why: Vinay Sitapati on why Narasimha Rao de­serves much of the credit for the 1991 re­forms, and on the re­form­ers around him.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s first-hand ac­count of his decades in the re­form en­gine room and the ‘silent revolution’ that built up from the late 1970s.

shelf.title: India’s Lost Decade (Episode 116, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Puja Mehra
shelf.why: Puja Mehra on what went wrong after 2008 and how the re­form era un­rav­elled, a com­pan­ion to her book The Lost Decade.

shelf.title: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (Episode 154, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay about their book In Service of the Republic and its frame­work for eco­nomic pol­icy.

shelf.title: The First Assault on Our Constitution (Episode 194) and Nehru’s Debates (Episode 262), The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh (and Adeel Hussain)
shelf.why: Tripurdaman Singh on the First Amendment to India’s Constitution, which Amit says badly harmed free speech in India: a con­ver­sa­tional way into the story Singh tells in Sixteen Stormy Days.

shelf.title: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Episode 7, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts go under the hood on how Newton and Gandhi emerged, trac­ing their in­tel­lec­tual in­flu­ences rather than judg­ing them by their high­light reels.

laughs.text: Amit opens by ex­plain­ing that a young cat is mew­ing in the back­ground, be­cause ‘it sounds like the wail­ing of all the dis­pos­sessed and the hun­gry and the starv­ing through these many, many years of India’s tor­mented jour­ney.’

Around 2008 Amit pitched a book called ‘Freedom After Midnight’, a play on Lapierre and Collins’s Freedom at Midnight, ar­gu­ing that 1947 brought only po­lit­i­cal free­dom. He never wrote it ‘be­cause I’m a lazy bum’, and the New India Foundation re­jected the pro­posal any­way.

Ajay lists the dan­gers of the 1940s, in­clud­ing ‘one minor char­ac­ter, Subhash Chandra Bose, threat­en­ing armed con­flict in India.’ Amit ob­jects, and Ajay re­tracts: ‘Fine. So scratch the Subhash Chandra Bose.’
On plan­ners who an­swered every fail­ure with more con­trols, Ajay says they in­sisted ‘the flog­gings will con­tinue until the morale im­proves.’
Nehru to J.R.D. Tata: ‘Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.’
